Naval Ravikant on the “single-most important indicator of an entrepreneur’s success”

Naval admits it’s very difficult to predict which startups will work—only 1 out of 10 of his angel investments succeed—but he has noticed a common trait among many of the great companies:

“The founders are in it for the long haul. And the way you see that evidence very early on. They are extremely deliberate about all kinds of small decisions. Stuff you might think that doesn’t matter… And what you realize is is it’s their nature to obsess over these things because they feel like like they’re laying the bricks and the foundation of a skyscraper.”

He contrasts this to entrepreneurs are more careless early on:

“The people who are flippant about things… they’re often signaling to you that they’ll sell the company the first chance they get, or the moment that it looks like they’re gonna run out of cash, they’ll shut down.”

He continues:

“So I think that long-term mentality is probably the single-most important indicator of an entrepreneur’s success. But it’s by no means the only thing. It’s a very competitive environment. Most startups fail. And so you just gotta stick with it.”

Video source: @StartupGrind (2013)

🧵 THE UNTOLD STORY OF DENELLE DIXON: FROM SMALL TOWN TO CRYPTO PIONEER 🧵

While everyone's focused on meme coins and price action, let me tell you about the INCREDIBLE woman revolutionizing global finance through @StellarOrg...

Growing up in tiny Gilroy, California (yes, the garlic capital), Denelle Dixon became the FIRST person in her family to attend college. No silver spoon, no tech connections - just determination to break barriers.

After earning her law degree from UC Hastings, she didn't follow the traditional path to a cushy firm. Instead, she dove into the world of technology, where few lawyers ventured at the time.

Her big break came at @Mozilla, where she rose from Associate General Counsel to Chief Operating Officer. While there, she fought fiercely for net neutrality and user privacy when most tech companies were selling out.

In 2019, she made a bold career pivot into blockchain, becoming CEO of the @StellarOrg Development Foundation. Not for the money or hype, but because she saw its potential to help those left behind by our financial system.

Under her leadership, Stellar partnered with @MoneyGram to build a bridge between crypto and cash - creating real on/off ramps for the 1.7 BILLION unbanked people worldwide.

But her most impactful work might be with Ukrainian refugees. Working with the Refugees (UNHCR), she helped develop Stellar Aid Assist, distributing essential funds via blockchain to those who lost everything to war.

Think about that for a second: people forced to flee their homes with nothing could instantly access financial aid without bank accounts, waiting in lines, or dealing with currency conversion.

While crypto bros were posting lambos, Denelle was quietly building systems that deliver aid to people in crisis zones within SECONDS instead of weeks.

Her vision isn't about pumps or dumps - it's about using blockchain to create a more inclusive financial system where anyone can participate, regardless of their background or location.

From a small town girl to a woman leading global financial innovation, her journey shows that the REAL revolution in crypto isn't about getting rich quick - it's about creating technology that serves humanity.

This is what actual leadership in blockchain looks like. Not hype. Not memes. But solving REAL problems for REAL people.

Follow @DenelleDixon if you want to see what's possible when technology meets purpose.

TAMMY CAMP: THE UNTOLD STORY OF CRYPTO'S MOST FASCINATING FOUNDER 🧵

Most crypto founders appeared during the ICO boom. Tammy Camp has been BUILDING since before most of us had internet access. Her journey from child prodigy to Stronghold CEO is WILD:

Born in the early 80s, Tammy was coding by AGE SIX on systems that saved data to cassette tapes. Think about that. While most kids were watching cartoons, she was writing code before Windows existed. This wasn't normal - especially for a girl in that era.

Her early start wasn't just a hobby. She developed genuine programming skills at an age when most people couldn't spell "computer." This natural affinity for technology would shape her entire career trajectory.

Fast forward to 2010 - while most people hadn't heard of Bitcoin, Tammy was at Singularity University's GSP11 program at NASA Ames Research Center. Not just any program - one focused on exponential technologies shaping the future.

John Collison explains why it’s important for founders to be curious

John recounts a story about Magnus Carlson winning a chess trivia contest:

“He knew the most chess trivia out of anyone in this contest, and I don’t think it’s a coincidence that the world’s number one player has also studied the most about chess history.”

As the Collison brothers scaled Stripe from two people to 7,000 people, they studied how other businesses navigated similar stages:

“I think you have to be curious about what is required to run a good company at that stage… One thing we try to do is just spend a lot of time looking at all the other companies and what they’ve done. Not that you want to blindly emulate them, but you should at least understand them.”

He gives Apple and Amazon as an example:

“You cannot imagine two companies that work more differently than the two of those… Yet they’re both really successful models. And so I think it’s useful to have a framework for how that stuff works.”

John also recommends trying to learn the best mental models from various domains and industries:

“I don’t know if every founder has to do it, but I do think it’s probably effective to be able to just know the top mental models from finance, engineering, product, sales, and stuff like that. I don’t see how you could be that effective without being pretty curious on how to learn the most important mental models from this particular domain or function.”

Video source: @MillionStories (2024)
